Messages.Author: Derek Ray
Messages.Body:
In message <3d697e44....@news.tcinternet.net>,
shan...@tcinternet.net (W. Mark Woodhouse) mumbled something about:



Yes.

I hardly see Swoop as useless, though. I have a couple decks that are
basically Flight/FOR, using POT only for the IG ability. Swoop + Pounce
provides you with a maneuver back to close and a hand strike for 4,
barring Depravity/etc.

In a close-range combat deck, you want to have maneuvers in case people
decide to run away from you. Swoop provides this, and gives you a bit
of "oomph" to your strength as well. Unflinching Persistence also
provides this, but gives you some damage prevention instead. Fake Out
sucks in comparison to each of these.

If people aren't running away from you, Fake Out and Swoop both have to
be discarded, while Unflinching Persistence can be burned as prevention
-- though if people are only punching you for 1, your other damage
prevention will start clogging your hand.

It all depends on which way you're wanting to go. Do you occasionally
need the extra strength? Or do you want the semi-free prevent?

As with everything, you can always make an argument when you picture the
game you want to play in your mind. In reality, Swoop's narrowness is hard
to love even in this kind of a deck. It's only a one-way maneuver - so
you're fucked if you suddenly decide you want to get away from the guy
who just Disguised out a Sengir Dagger. And you can't use more than one of
them in a round. And what to you get if you manage to use _exactly_ _one_
of the them - no more, no less - to get you to close range? ONE STRENGTH.
Whoop-de-whoop. Oh, boy, what a killer!

The stupid things might have been slightly interesting if they'd gotten
rid of the one-per-round limitation and the only-maneuver-to-close
limitation and substituted something that said you only get +1 strength
once per round and only get it if you maneuver to close. Then, you could
go to town with them and not worry about ever regretting using them in
preference to Fake Outs. As it is, Fakes Out are certainly much better.

Fred

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
"Frederick Scott" <freds64_at_...@removethis.com> wrote in message
news:3D6A6A0A...@removethis.com...

>

> "problem" I was referring to was the same one you're using Swoop to solve:
> closing on long range combat decks.
>

Umm... what?

Maneuvers are *not* an effective way of dealing with long range combat decks.
They just have too many maneuvers. More effective ways are to set range, not
allow them to maneuver to long (i.e. with Drawing Out the Beast), to pack your
own long range combat, or else have some combat defense.

Maneuvers are essential to a close range combat deck (especially one with
Immortal Grapple), to deal with combat *defense*. They maneuver to long, you
can't grapple them, and they have the option of whether to let you wave or
cycle a S:CE. Such decks rarely have tons of maneuvers, or else they would
choke on them. Nossies can use Behind You or Drawing Out the Beast to solve
this problem, but the Gargoyles really have only 2 options: Swoop and
Unflinching Persistance. Unflinching Persistance is often better, but requires
superior fortitude.

Like the a previous argument I got into with Derek, I disagree with a lot of
these statements from what I believe is either differing experience or an
essentially differing philosophical outlook.

There's no point in differentiating "combat defense" from "combat" for this
purpose. There's no hard and fast dividing line when someone might pack Thrown
Gates primarily to run away from you and if they tink you for one, that's gravy.
On the other hand, they might also start loading up on the Increased Strengths
to actually cause damage. It's silly to look into someone's head and try and
decide if his maneuvers are "offense" or "defense" and by these means attempt
to divine how many maneuvers he's packing.

As for "choking" on maneuvers, don't they have a discard phase where some of
you guys come from?

Fred

If you're a Nossie vote deck trying to get away from me with a Thrown
Gate, then the Swoop in my hand catches you and you get pounded -- and I
don't even GET hit for 1 in the process (meaning I probably don't
Grapple you, so I can play some prevent).

If I don't have ANY maneuvers in my deck, I sit there with my thumb up
my butt and look silly -- decreasing my deck's effectiveness for no good
reason.

If you're a Brujah pitch deck leading off with a Thrown Gate, then you
already have a Flash and Pursuit in hand, and I'm not going to catch you
no matter what I do -- but at least I can play my Swoop, even though
it's pointless.

That's the difference.

>On the other hand, they might also start loading up on the Increased Strengths
>to actually cause damage. It's silly to look into someone's head and try and

Increased Strength, being played before-range, will let me know whether
that's an "offensive" or "defensive" Thrown Gate.

>decide if his maneuvers are "offense" or "defense" and by these means attempt
>to divine how many maneuvers he's packing.

A Thrown Gate is almost always a "defensive" maneuver. In the rare
instances where it's offensive, it's backed up by Carrion
Crows/Increased Strength (pre-range, therefore tipping you off), or by
Blurs and Lids (you're fighting the Brujah, and it is safe to assume
that clan is playing "offensive" combat).

I realize this is only one particular example, but it's pretty easy to
tell whether someone is trying to run away from you, or stepping back to
take aim. And in any case, it doesn't really matter -- you've built
your deck to chase down casual maneuvers, and if they have
tons-o-maneuvers, you might as well cycle yours out of your hand, since
you won't ever catch them anyway.

>As for "choking" on maneuvers, don't they have a discard phase where some of
>you guys come from?

You only get 12 of those per game. If 8 of them are occupied by
maneuver cards, you don't get to use it very much to actually improve
your hand, or deal with OTHER (Master) types of hand-jam.

> >you guys come from?

Chris's actual comment was about having, "a ton of maneuvers", which was
actually probably reasonable enough. In other words, I'm changing my objection
to what he said by writing this. But you wouldn't have a huge number of them.
I don't think you need a bunch of them - only enough to cancel out the handful of
Swoops a Gargoyle deck would use.

> You only get 12 of those per game. If 8 of them are occupied by
> maneuver cards, you don't get to use it very much to actually improve
> your hand, or deal with OTHER (Master) types of hand-jam.

Nor sure where you got 12 but I'll assume you're averaging turns/game or
something. The point is, you only get one per turn (assuming no Barrens,
Dreams, or whatever); I realize that. I agree, you don't want to spend them
on something like this if you don't have to. On the other hand, the extra
combat defense helps you survive, well, just this sort of thing: a relatively
small quantity of maneuvers thrown into a combat deck. The penalty that you
sometimes have to burn some discard phases when you don't need doesn't seem to
be all that bad to me. For one thing, you can often control your own capacity
to get into combat (e.g. against an SCE deck or other basically defensive deck)
and dump them. You can also maneuver with the Fake Out and then throw the gate
anyway to dump extra maneuvers. It's not like if you run up against the wrong
deck, you're always just stuck with them and have to discard them.

Fred

Token defense often defaults to a bunch of Fake Outs and some Dodges, or
some Zip Guns, or some Thrown Gates if you have Potence... or... take
your pick. A maneuver is often better than S:CE, especially with the

Flash and Pursuit are the primary two CEL utility cards. One is a

Trying to be 100% certain about things before you try them leads to,

anything with a fair amount of their own maneuvers (whether because they're
"combat" vs. "combat defense" decks I don't care), they generally fail and

Absolutely. But I sure don't see why ranged-combat-DEFENSE doesn't want to avoid
being grappled and killed as well. Especially given that extra maneuvers can
also be used as extra combat defense if what they're facing doesn't have its own
maneuvers. That is, you have both maneuvers and Gates in your deck and you see
your opponent has no maneuvers (so far, after he's gone through 40% of his deck),
so now you can let up on avoiding combat somewhat. You can take more actions
you know are blockable and start putting more pressure on his ability to play
intercept or wakes or both even knowing you'll be intercepted and be in combat
more often. If he has the maneuvers, you're more careful because you can still
survive combat using both Gates and maneuvers but not as often, as you'll burn
through more combat cards per combat.

You need a Gate - which you have anyway for defense - and a separate maneuver. A
single separate maneuver cancels the "single Swoop". That's 6 against 6. And
if you don't run into maneuvers, you have 6 more combat defense cards and can
allow yourself to get into a few more combats, as above.

Fred

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:

> defense, or you could have both. I'm saying that out of all these decks, I
find
> that the number of them that use maneuver to get away from close combat for
> whatever reason aren't that common.
>

That's where you'd be wrong. Since you're grappling, their *only* defense is
to maneuver away, or else to prevent. Many clans cannot prevent, leaving
maneuver away as their only option. Even if you're, for some odd reason,
playing in an environment where no one grapples, so no one maneuvers away,
after playing your Gargoyle deck a few times, people will at least see the
possibility. If the deck is any good, the metagame will adjust to adding
maneuver away as an option. Heck, maneuver away is the primary combat defense
in *most* of my decks - S:CE is just not reliable by itself.

Messages.Author: Dan Harting
Messages.Body:
Frederick Scott wrote:

> There's no point in differentiating "combat defense" from "combat" for this
> purpose. There's no hard and fast dividing line when someone might pack
> Thrown Gates primarily to run away from you and if they tink you for one,
> that's gravy. On the other hand, they might also start loading up on the
> Increased Strengths to actually cause damage. It's silly to look into
> someone's head and try and decide if his maneuvers are "offense" or "defense"
> and by these means attempt to divine how many maneuvers he's packing.

> Fred

I don't mean to disagree with your other points, and I do think
that it is dangerous to assume contents of your opponent's deck
based on categorization - though it is good VTES to try to
piece together what they are doing - but it does seem that a deck's
devotion or nod given to combat is qualifiable.

If you think doing one damage is an accomplishment,
your combat might be defensive.

If you have a card that says "dodge" in your hand but
none that say "additional strike" or "press",
your combat might be defensive.

If you end combat and don't continue your rush at +1
stealth (stealth optional),
your combat might be defensive.

If you maneuver and don't have a ranged strike,
your combat might be defensive.

If you have doubts about blocking or taking an
action because the block might succeed,
your combat might be defensive.

- Dan Harting

> Since you're grappling, their *only* defense

What's "since I'm grappling" got to do with anything. People build their decks

lots of people _I_ play apparently do.

> is to maneuver away, or else to prevent. Many clans cannot prevent, leaving

Yea, but big deal. It's only one deck. It's not like people will see this one
deck that grapples all the time and instantly go out and reformat all their
decks out of terror of it. Certainly not by throwing a handful of maneuvers
into their decks, and throwing just a few in only means you'll get away from
the thug once in a while. The rest of time, you suffer. Better to just ignore
the possibility until you start to see lots of Grapple deck in your environment.

> Heck, maneuver away is the primary combat defense
> in *most* of my decks - S:CE is just not reliable by itself.

That's odd. I've always considered S:CE to be much more reliable of the two.
Too many Gun decks and too many people throwing the odd Ivory Bow or Flamethrower
into otherwise peaceful decks. (I really got "up close and personal" experience
with the horror of Watenda holding an Ivory Bow at Gencon. Several different
games. At least it works to S:CE if you hold _two_ of them going in...) Or,
hell, how about Thrown Gates with Increased Strengths, since we're on the subject.
Trap decks. Tremere combat decks. Assamite long range combat decks. There's
probably others but I've made my point. Again, it just depends on how the other
guys you play with like to play their games.

Fred
